extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, and readers of Retraction Watch interested in preprint integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and reporting problems with arXiv preprints (e.g., AI‑generated text, authorship disputes, duplication, unusual citation behavior) and documenting reasons for withdrawal. The page is a news roundup highlighting specific cases and signals used by the community to flag problematic preprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-generated phrases indicate AI use
rubrics_metrics.description: These phrases indicate AI use and occur when large language models try to find synonyms for common phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the article: 'linear regression' became 'straight relapse', 'error rate' became 'blunder rate', and odd phrases like 'squared blunder' and 'info picture' were flagged. Detection occurred via PubPeer commentary and tools such as the Problematic Paper Screener; tortured or unnatural synonym substitutions are highlighted as signals of LLM involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community sleuthing and PubPeer commentary as a detection mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems with preprints are often identified by external commenters and sleuths on platforms like PubPeer rather than by the server itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites Guillaume Cabanac (creator of the Problematic Paper Screener) and PubPeer commenters who pointed out AI-like phrases; community-posted observations can prompt author responses or withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should disclose use of AI / transparency about provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Author behavior around admitting or concealing AI assistance is a factor in how a preprint is received; undisclosed or problematic AI use can lead to censure or withdrawal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the featured case the author admitted using AI to 'help write' the preprint and described it as a 'personal learning exercise'; the admission followed community flagging and preceded withdrawal. While the page is a report rather than a policy, it implies transparency about AI assistance matters to community trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial text overlap / duplication is problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant overlap in text between versions or with other works is treated as a concern and can precipitate withdrawal or disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The math preprint example notes 'substantial text overlap' between two versions; one co-author requested withdrawal and another posted his own version. Such overlap is presented as a substantive trigger for conflict and removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship disputes (irreconcilable differences) justify withdrawal
rubrics_metrics.description: When co-authors are 'severely at odds' or have an 'irreconcilable difference of opinion', a paper may be withdrawn from the preprint server.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page quotes an arXiv withdrawal note citing an 'irreconcilable difference of opinion' and describes how disagreement between co-authors led to competing versions and a requested withdrawal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusual bibliometric behavior (self-citation) is noteworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale or concentrated instances of self-citation across papers/journals are identified as a phenomenon meriting scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article summarizes research finding 'just under 45,000 academic papers contained citations to themselves', with many journals and a subset of publications accounting for disproportionate shares. While not a prescriptive rule, the piece treats excessive self-citation as a signal worth reporting and investigating.
